claim: At excitatory synapses, glutamatergic receptors activated by spontaneous and evoked neurotransmission are segregated.
source: At excitatory synapses, glutamatergic receptors activated by spontaneous and evoked neurotransmission are segregated.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work in the field.

claim: Inhibitory synapses differ from excitatory synapses in both structure and function.
source: Although inhibitory synapses also transmit signals spontaneously or in response to action potentials, they differ from excitatory synapses in both structure and function.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Picrotoxin is a GABAAR antagonist that blocks neurotransmission in a use-dependent manner at rat hippocampal synapses.
source: We report picrotoxin, a GABAAR antagonist, blocks neurotransmission in a use-dependent manner at rat hippocampal synapses and therefore can be used to interrogate synaptic properties.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Up to 40% of the evoked response is mediated through GABAARs which are only activated by evoked neurotransmission.
source: We found up to 40% of the evoked response is mediated through GABAARs which are only activated by evoked neurotransmission.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: GABAergic spontaneous and evoked neurotransmission processes are partially non-overlapping.
source: These data indicate GABAergic spontaneous and evoked neurotransmission processes are partially non-overlapping, suggesting they may serve divergent roles in neuronal signaling.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Evoked neurotransmission is the canonical action-potential driven signaling that causes synchronous or asynchronous release of vesicles at multiple synapses.
source: Evoked neurotransmission is the canonical action-potential driven signaling that causes synchronous or asynchronous release of vesicles at multiple synapses (Südhof, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Spontaneous neurotransmission occurs via action-potential independent release of single synaptic vesicles.
source: Spontaneous neurotransmission occurs via action-potential independent release of single synaptic vesicles.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Spontaneous neurotransmission has been shown to utilize partly different molecular machinery and act at distinct postsynaptic sites than evoked neurotransmission.
source: At the molecular level, spontaneous neurotransmission has been shown to utilize partly different molecular machinery and act at distinct postsynaptic sites than evoked neurotransmission (Kavalali, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Spontaneous and evoked glutamate release at excitatory synapses in the hippocampus activate distinct sets of AMPA receptors.
source: Spontaneous and evoked glutamate release at excitatory synapses in the hippocampus, as well as synapses at the Drosophila neuromuscular junction, activate distinct sets of α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid (AMPA) receptors (Melom et al., 2013; Peled et al., 2014; Sara et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Synaptic NMDA receptors in the hippocampus show a near complete segregation in their responses to spontaneous and evoked glutamate release.
source: Synaptic N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptors in the hippocampus also show a near complete segregation in their responses to spontaneous and evoked glutamate release (Atasoy et al., 2008; Reese and Kavalali, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Spontaneous and evoked neurotransmission can occur at the same synapse but activate separate NMDA and AMPA receptors.
source: These studies have demonstrated that spontaneous and evoked neurotransmission can occur at the same synapse; nevertheless, these different forms of transmission activate separate NMDA and AMPA receptors.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: There are clear and distinct differences in downstream signaling between evoked and spontaneous neurotransmission at excitatory synapses.
source: Segregation may be necessary due to the clear and distinct differences in downstream signaling between evoked and spontaneous neurotransmission at excitatory synapses (Autry et al., 2011; Crawford et al., 2017; Fong et al., 2015; Gonzalez-Islas et al., 2018; Nosyreva et al., 2013; Ramirez et al., 2017; Sutton et al., 2006; Sutton et al., 2007; Sutton et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claim: Inhibitory neurotransmission serves distinct functions in circuits, targets different neuronal sites, and partly relies on separate presynaptic and postsynaptic molecular machineries compared to excitatory neurotransmission.
source: In contrast to excitatory neurotransmission, inhibitory neurotransmission serves distinct functions in circuits, targets different neuronal sites, and partly relies on separate presynaptic and postsynaptic molecular machineries (Courtney et al., 2018; Higley, 2014; Tyagarajan and Fritschy, 2014; Williams and Smith, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Picrotoxin is a commonly used noncompetitive GABAAR antagonist.
source: Picrotoxin (PTX) is a commonly used noncompetitive GABAAR antagonist (Akaike et al., 1985; Gallagher et al., 1978; Nicoll and Wojtowicz, 1980; Takeuchi and Takeuchi, 1969).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Structural evidence suggests PTX binds within the pore of the GABAAR.
source: Structural evidence suggests PTX binds within the pore of the GABAAR (Chen et al., 2006; Gurley et al., 1995; Hibbs and Gouaux, 2011; Masiulis et al., 2019; Olsen, 2006), and may act in a use-dependent manner to block GABAAR channels (Akaike et al., 1985; Newland and Cull-Candy, 1992; Yoon et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: PTX may act in a use-dependent manner to block GABAAR channels.
source: Structural evidence suggests PTX binds within the pore of the GABAAR (Chen et al., 2006; Gurley et al., 1995; Hibbs and Gouaux, 2011; Masiulis et al., 2019; Olsen, 2006), and may act in a use-dependent manner to block GABAAR channels (Akaike et al., 1985; Newland and Cull-Candy, 1992; Yoon et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Previous studies used exogenously applied GABA to examine the pharmacology of PTX, which may not be completely relevant to physiological signaling mediated by synaptically released GABA.
source: However, previous studies used exogenously applied GABA to examine the pharmacology of PTX; this setting may not be completely relevant to physiological signaling mediated by synaptically released GABA.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of prior work based on inference.

claim: Both spontaneous and evoked currents had faster decay times after PTX treatment.
source: Both spontaneous and evoked currents had faster decay times after PTX (Figure 1A–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: 50 µM of PTX was able to completely abolish spontaneous miniature inhibitory postsynaptic currents (mIPSCs) within 5 min of application.
source: Here and all subsequent experiments, we used 50 µM of PTX as this concentration of PTX was able to completely abolish spontaneous miniature inhibitory postsynaptic currents (mIPSCs) within 5 min of application (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, also see below).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Stimulating hippocampal synapses at a variety of frequencies and measuring the evoked IPSC peak amplitudes in the presence of PTX resulted in a response that decreased as a function of stimulation number regardless of PTX incubation time.
source: Under the same conditions, stimulating hippocampal synapses at a variety of frequencies and measuring the evoked IPSC (eIPSC) peak amplitudes in the presence of PTX resulted in a response that decreased as a function of stimulation number regardless of PTX incubation time, indicating PTX is a use-dependent antagonist (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Stimulation in the absence of PTX led to a small decrease in eIPSC peak amplitude which was far less than the decrease in the presence of PTX, and may reflect metabolic rundown.
source: In contrast, stimulation in the absence of PTX led to a small decrease in eIPSC peak amplitude which was far less than the decrease in the presence of PTX, and may reflect metabolic rundown.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and includes speculative reasoning about metabolic rundown.

claim: The rate of GABAAR block should be proportional to presynaptic release probability if picrotoxin is truly a use-dependent antagonist.
source: If picrotoxin is truly a use-dependent antagonist, then the rate of GABAAR block should be proportional to presynaptic release probability (as with MK801 and NMDA receptors; Hessler et al., 1993; Rosenmund et al., 1993).
evidence: This is based on inference from prior work with MK801 and NMDA receptors.

claim: Increasing Ca2+ concentration (from 0.5 mM – 8 mM) led to an increase in the initial eIPSC response to evoked stimulation.
source: Increasing Ca2+ concentration (from 0.5 mM – 8 mM) led to an increase in the initial eIPSC response to evoked stimulation (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Increasing Ca2+ concentration led to a decrease in paired pulse ratio and switched synapses from facilitation to depression, which is consistent with an increase in release probability.
source: Moreover, increasing Ca2+ concentration led to a decrease in paired pulse ratio and switched synapses from facilitation to depression, which is consistent with an increase in release probability (Figure 2A,C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2 and interpreted based on established knowledge.

claim: Increasing release probability, via increasing external Ca2+ concentration, reliably led to a more rapid block of the eIPSC response.
source: Increasing release probability, via increasing external Ca2+ concentration, reliably led to a more rapid block of the eIPSC response (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: PTX acts as a use-dependent blocker and can be used to monitor alterations in presynaptic release probability at inhibitory synapses.
source: These data demonstrate that PTX acts as a use-dependent blocker and can be used to monitor alterations in presynaptic release probability at inhibitory synapses.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental data presented in Figure 2.

claim: 5 min of PTX treatment in the absence of stimulation was sufficient to fully block the mIPSCs.
source: When measuring the time course of mIPSC block in PTX, we found that 5 min of PTX treatment in the absence of stimulation was sufficient to fully block the mIPSCs (Figure 3B–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B-C.

claim: Both the frequency and amplitude distributions of spontaneous events were unaltered by the addition of tetrodotoxin (TTX), indicating that suppression of excitatory synaptic transmission to isolate inhibitory neurotransmission is in itself sufficient to block all network activity.
source: Both the frequency and amplitude distributions of these spontaneous events were unaltered by the addition of tetrodotoxin (TTX), indicating that suppression of excitatory synaptic transmission to isolate inhibitory neurotransmission is in itself sufficient to block all network activity and enable detection of mIPSCs without a requirement for TTX application (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Augmented mIPSCs recorded using the high Cl- internal solution followed a similar time course of block in the presence of PTX as those recorded using the standard internal solution.
source: Augmented mIPSCs recorded using the high Cl- internal solution followed a similar time course of block in the presence of PTX as those recorded using the standard internal solution (Figure 3B–C), indicating that GABAARs which are activated by spontaneous signaling have reached a steady state of block following a 5 min incubation in PTX.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B-C.

claim: Because PTX is use-dependent, and nearly all spontaneous responses are suppressed after a 5 min incubation, the majority of remaining response to evoked stimulation after 5 min must be mediated by GABAARs which are only responsive to evoked neurotransmission.
source: Because PTX is use-dependent, and nearly all spontaneous responses are suppressed after a 5 min incubation (Figure 3B), the majority of remaining response to evoked stimulation after 5 min must be mediated by GABAARs which are only responsive to evoked neurotransmission.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data and the use-dependent properties of PTX.

claim: After 5 min in PTX, when all receptors activated by mIPSCs are blocked, the unblocked evoked response is 40.1 ± 9.6% of the maximum response.
source: After 5 min in PTX, when all receptors activated by mIPSCs are blocked, the unblocked evoked response is 40.1 ± 9.6% of the maximum response.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: The magnitude of the remaining evoked response was remarkably similar if the cells were incubated at rest with PTX for 8 min (39.7 ± 4.6%).
source: The magnitude of the remaining evoked response was remarkably similar if the cells were incubated at rest with PTX for 8 min (39.7 ± 4.6%, Figure 3H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Approximately 40% of the evoked inhibitory response is mediated by postsynaptic GABAARs which are exclusively activated by evoked neurotransmission, while the remaining 60% of the response is mediated by receptors which are activated by both spontaneous and evoked neurotransmission in hippocampal cultures.
source: This result indicates that approximately 40% of the evoked inhibitory response is mediated by postsynaptic GABAARs which are exclusively activated by evoked neurotransmission, while the remaining 60% of the response is mediated by receptors which are activated by both spontaneous and evoked neurotransmission in hippocampal cultures.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental data presented in Figure 3.

claim: Increasing extracellular Ca2+ concentration between 0.5 mM, 1 mM, and 2 mM caused an increase in release probability in hippocampal slices, as indicated by a decrease in paired pulse ratio and increase in initial peak amplitude of fIPSPs.
source: Increasing extracellular Ca2+ concentration between 0.5 mM, 1 mM, and 2 mM caused an increase in release probability, as indicated by a decrease in paired pulse ratio (Figure 4B–C) and increase in initial peak amplitude of fIPSPs (Figure 4B,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: In the presence of PTX to block GABAARs, greater release probability caused an increase in the rate of GABAAR block as evidenced by a faster and more pronounced decline in peak amplitude of fIPSPs.
source: In the presence of PTX to block GABAARs, greater release probability caused an increase in the rate of GABAAR block as evidenced by a faster and more pronounced decline in peak amplitude of fIPSPs (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: PTX is use-dependent and can be used to compare release probability across different conditions in hippocampal slice recordings.
source: These data support our earlier conclusions by demonstrating that PTX is use-dependent and can be used to compare release probability across different conditions in hippocampal slice recordings.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental data presented in Figure 4.

claim: Following 10 min of PTX application at rest, when most receptors activated by spontaneous signaling are expected to be suppressed, there is a remaining evoked response, suggesting that this response is mediated by GABAARs activated specifically by evoked stimulation.
source: Conversely, following 10 min of PTX application at rest, when most receptors activated by spontaneous signaling are expected to be suppressed, there is a remaining evoked response, suggesting that this response is mediated by GABAARs activated specifically by evoked stimulation consistent with our prior findings.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and inference from the use-dependent properties of PTX.

claim: The remaining evoked response in hippocampal slices following 10 min of PTX application at rest was similar in magnitude to results in culture (34.05 ± 5.37%).
source: Remarkably, this remaining response was similar in magnitude to our results in culture (34.05 ± 5.37%).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: The eIPSC response was greatly diminished when 55 mM of KCl alone was applied for 90 s, likely due to rapid depletion of vesicle pools.
source: As expected, the eIPSC response was greatly diminished when 55 mM of KCl alone was applied for 90 s, likely due to rapid depletion of vesicle pools (Sara et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observation and citation to prior work.

claim: eIPSC responses following 55 mM of KCl with PTX treatment recovered following successive stimulations, however the recovery occurred over a longer time period, consistent with the premise that blocked receptors were gradually unblocked by successive stimulations.
source: eIPSC responses following 55 mM of KCl with PTX treatment also recovered following successive stimulations, however the recovery occurred over a longer time period, consistent with the premise that blocked receptors were gradually unblocked by successive stimulations (Figure 5B–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B-C.

claim: PTX unblock from GABAARs has been shown to be at least partially use-dependent.
source: This finding agrees with previous studies (Newland and Cull-Candy, 1992) where PTX unblock from GABAARs has been shown to be at least partially use-dependent (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work and experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Following application of 55 mM of KCl, mIPSC responses were partly diminished, but then recovered back to a steady baseline.
source: Following application of 55 mM of KCl, mIPSC responses were partly diminished, but then recovered back to a steady baseline (Figure 5D–E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D-E.

claim: When 55 mM of KCl was co-applied with PTX, mIPSC responses were greatly diminished, indicating GABAARs activated by spontaneous release were blocked by 55 mM of KCl and PTX co-application.
source: When 55 mM of KCl was co-applied with PTX, mIPSC responses were greatly diminished, indicating GABAARs activated by spontaneous release were blocked by 55 mM of KCl and PTX co-application.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and inference.

claim: The recovery of mIPSCs in cells treated with 55 mM of KCl and PTX in the absence of stimulation was slow and minimal.
source: The recovery of mIPSCs in cells treated with 55 mM of KCl and PTX in the absence of stimulation was slow and minimal (Figure 5D–E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D-E.

claim: The spontaneous release rate per synapse is in the order of 1 vesicle per minute per synapse.
source: This is not surprising since the spontaneous release rate per synapse is in the order of 1 vesicle per minute per synapse (Leitz and Kavalali, 2014; Sara et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The presence of 0.2 Hz stimulation significantly increased the recovery of mIPSCs following GABAAR block with KCl and PTX, indicating that evoked release activates some of the same GABAARs as spontaneous release.
source: However, the presence of 0.2 Hz stimulation significantly increased the recovery of mIPSCs (Figure 5F), indicating that evoked release activates some of the same GABAARs as spontaneous release.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Stimulation significantly increased the recovery of mIPSCs following GABAAR block using muscimol and PTX.
source: We obtained similar results using this approach, that is stimulation significantly increased the recovery of mIPSCs following GABAAR block (Figure 6D–E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D-E.

claim: GABAARs which are activated by spontaneous and evoked release partially overlap, but do not exclude the existence of a fraction of GABAARs which are only activated by spontaneous release.
source: These results support the notion that GABAARs which are activated by spontaneous and evoked release partially overlap, but do not exclude the existence of a fraction of GABAARs which are only activated by spontaneous release.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental data presented in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: PTX does not simply block pore conductance of GABA channels but rather binds to a site within the pore to stabilize a closed state.
source: However, it is important to caution that PTX does not simply block pore conductance of GABA channels but rather binds to a site within the pore to stabilize a closed state (Masiulis et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to structural studies.

claim: Recovery from PTX block is only partially use-dependent.
source: In addition, recovery from block is only partially use-dependent as indicated by earlier work (Newland and Cull-Candy, 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Evoked and spontaneous neurotransmission processes are partially segregated at inhibitory synapses.
source: Our results show that evoked and spontaneous neurotransmission processes are partially segregated at inhibitory synapses.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: 34–40% of the total evoked GABAergic response recorded at the stratum pyramidale of hippocampal CA1 region and in hippocampal cultures is mediated by receptors which are only activated by evoked neurotransmission.
source: We estimate that 34–40% of the total evoked GABAergic response recorded at the stratum pyramidale of hippocampal CA1 region and in hippocampal cultures is mediated by receptors which are only activated by evoked neurotransmission.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding supported by experimental data from both culture and slice experiments.

claim: mIPSC recovery following GABAAR block was enhanced by the presence of stimulation, but these results do not exclude the possibility that some GABAARs are only activated by spontaneous release.
source: Although mIPSC recovery following GABAAR block was enhanced by the presence of stimulation, these results do not exclude the possibility that some GABAARs are only activated by spontaneous release and account for the population that recovers in the absence of stimulation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data that acknowledges alternative possibilities.

claim: Synapses are organized into 'nano-columns' such that a single vesicle only activates juxtaposed receptors on the postsynaptic membrane.
source: A growing body of evidence suggests that synapses are organized into 'nano-columns' such that a single vesicle only activates juxtaposed receptors on the postsynaptic membrane (Biederer et al., 2017; Maschi and Klyachko, 2017; Tang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Segregation may be achieved through a combination of differential presynaptic molecular regulation and pre/postsynaptic spatial separation within the same synapse.
source: One model posits that segregation is achieved through a combination of differential presynaptic molecular regulation and pre/postsynaptic spatial separation within the same synapse.
evidence: This is a speculative model proposed to explain the findings.

claim: Segregation may arise through differential action of presynaptic and postsynaptic mechanisms over different inhibitory synapses.
source: Alternatively, segregation may arise through differential action of these mechanisms over different inhibitory synapses.
evidence: This is a speculative alternative model proposed to explain the findings.

claim: Excitatory synapses can exhibit both spontaneous and evoked release while others exclusively exhibit spontaneous or evoked release.
source: Earlier studies demonstrated that excitatory synapses can exhibit both spontaneous and evoked release while others exclusively exhibit spontaneous or evoked release (Leitz and Kavalali, 2014; Melom et al., 2013; Peled et al., 2014; Reese and Kavalali, 2016; Walter et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: There may be more overlap in the molecular machinery used for spontaneous and evoked neurotransmission at inhibitory synapses compared to excitatory synapses.
source: First, there may be more overlap in the molecular machinery used for spontaneous and evoked neurotransmission at inhibitory synapses.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed partial segregation.

claim: Synaptic vesicle pools mediating spontaneous and evoked release may be distinct at inhibitory synapses.
source: Although earlier work has suggested that synaptic vesicle pools mediating spontaneous and evoked release may be distinct at inhibitory synapses (Chung et al., 2010), unlike at excitatory synapses, spontaneous release at inhibitory synapses is partly coupled to activation of voltage activated Ca2+ channels (Tsintsadze et al., 2017; Vyleta and Smith, 2011; Williams and Smith, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Spontaneous release at inhibitory synapses is partly coupled to activation of voltage activated Ca2+ channels.
source: Although earlier work has suggested that synaptic vesicle pools mediating spontaneous and evoked release may be distinct at inhibitory synapses (Chung et al., 2010), unlike at excitatory synapses, spontaneous release at inhibitory synapses is partly coupled to activation of voltage activated Ca2+ channels (Tsintsadze et al., 2017; Vyleta and Smith, 2011; Williams and Smith, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Synaptotagmin-1, the canonical Ca2+ sensor for fast synchronous evoked release, also regulates Ca2+ dependent spontaneous release, but only at inhibitory synapses.
source: Moreover, recent evidence suggests that synaptotagmin-1, the canonical Ca2+ sensor for fast synchronous evoked release (Geppert et al., 1994), also regulates Ca2+ dependent spontaneous release, but only at inhibitory synapses (Courtney et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Unlike Ca2+ signaling through NMDA receptors, chloride flow through GABAARs has very few targets that may direct downstream biochemical signaling.
source: Second, unlike Ca2+ signaling through NMDA receptors, chloride flow through GABAARs has very few targets that may direct downstream biochemical signaling (Chen et al., 2019; Heubl et al., 2017; Piala et al., 2014), although GABAergic transmission has been shown to indirectly regulate dendritic Ca2+ signaling (Chiu et al., 2013; Higley, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: GABAergic transmission has been shown to indirectly regulate dendritic Ca2+ signaling.
source: Second, unlike Ca2+ signaling through NMDA receptors, chloride flow through GABAARs has very few targets that may direct downstream biochemical signaling (Chen et al., 2019; Heubl et al., 2017; Piala et al., 2014), although GABAergic transmission has been shown to indirectly regulate dendritic Ca2+ signaling (Chiu et al., 2013; Higley, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The strong segregation that is seen at excitatory synapses may not be as essential to mediate inhibitory synaptic communication.
source: Therefore, the strong segregation that is seen at excitatory synapses may not be as essential to mediate inhibitory synaptic communication.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed partial segregation at inhibitory synapses.

claim: The postsynaptic organization of inhibitory synapses shows only partial segregation of GABAARs that respond to evoked and spontaneous neurotransmission, suggesting a distinct organizing principle of these synapses compared to their excitatory counterparts.
source: Our current findings provide evidence that the postsynaptic organization of inhibitory synapses shows only partial segregation of GABAARs that respond to evoked and spontaneous neurotransmission (Figure 6F), suggesting a distinct organizing principle of these synapses compared to their excitatory counterparts.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Even partial segregation at inhibitory synapses may provide a platform for differential signaling by evoked and spontaneous GABAergic neurotransmission in the central nervous system.
source: Nevertheless, given recently identified targets for chloride-mediated biochemical signaling in neurons (Chen et al., 2019; Heubl et al., 2017; Piala et al., 2014), even this partial segregation may provide a platform for differential signaling by evoked and spontaneous GABAergic neurotransmission in the central nervous system.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings in light of recent discoveries.

claim: Dissociated hippocampal cultures were prepared from PN1-3 rats.
source: Dissociated hippocampal cultures were prepared as previously described (Kavalali et al., 1999). Briefly, whole hippocampi were dissected from PN1-3 rats, trypsinized (~4 mg/mL, Sigma), mechanically dissociated, and plated on matrigel (BD Biosciences) coated glass coverslips.
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the experimental procedures.

claim: Electrophysiology was performed on DIV15-21 cells using the whole cell voltage clamp configuration.
source: On DIV15-21 cells were recorded using the whole cell voltage clamp configuration of the patch clamp technique.
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the experimental procedures.

claim: Cells were held at −70 mV and liquid junction potential was not corrected for.
source: Cells were held at −70 mV and liquid junction potential was not corrected for.
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the experimental procedures.

claim: eIPSCs were on the order of 2–4 nA.
source: eIPSCs were on the order of 2–4 nA.
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the experimental measurements.

claim: Series resistance compensation was not employed in these experiments and series resistance measures were 10 MΩ or below.
source: Series resistance compensation was not employed in these experiments and series resistance measures were 10 MΩ or below.
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the experimental procedures.

claim: Adult female dam rats aged 11–13 weeks were used for all hippocampal slice experiments.
source: Adult female dam rats aged 11–13 weeks were used for all hippocampal slice experiments.
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the experimental subjects.

claim: No more than four hippocampal slices were used per dam, and each experiment was performed on slices from at least two different animals.
source: No more than four hippocampal slices were used per dam, and each experiment was performed on slices from at least two different animals.
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the experimental design.

claim: Hippocampi were cut with a vibratome into 400 μm-thick transverse sections.
source: Hippocampi were dissected and cut with a vibratome into 400 μm-thick transverse sections in ice-cold dissection buffer continuously aerated with 95% O2 and 5% CO2.
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the experimental procedures.

claim: Area CA3 was surgically removed immediately after sectioning.
source: Area CA3 was surgically removed immediately after sectioning.
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the experimental procedures.

claim: Sections were recovered for 3–6 hr at 30°C in oxygenated artificial cerebrospinal fluid (ACSF).
source: Sections were recovered for 3–6 hr at 30°C in oxygenated artificial cerebrospinal fluid (ACSF) containing the following: 124 mM of NaCl, 5 mM of KCl, 1.25 mM of NaH2PO4, 26 mM of NaHCO3, 2 mM of CaCl2, 1 mM of MgCl2 and 10 mM of glucose, pH 7.4 (continuously aerated with 95% O2 and 5% CO2).
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the experimental procedures.

claim: 25 μM of D-APV and 10 μM of NBQX were added to the ACSF to block NMDA and AMPA channels, respectively, and isolate inhibitory GABA-mediated currents.
source: 25 μM of D-APV and 10 μM of NBQX were added to the ACSF to block NMDA and AMPA channels, respectively, and isolate inhibitory GABA-mediated currents.
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the experimental procedures.

claim: Bicuculline did not further decrease the measured response after PTX application, indicating that PTX blocked the full range of the GABAAR-mediated response.
source: Following the conclusion of these experiments, bicuculline was applied to confirm the range of inhibitory response. Bicuculline did not further decrease the measured response, indicating that as for dissociated culture experiments, PTX blocked the full range of the GABAAR-mediated response.
evidence: This is a methodological validation supported by experimental observation.

claim: Field Inhibitory Postsynaptic Potentials (fIPSPs) were evoked by inserting a concentric bipolar stimulating electrode and an extracellular recording electrode filled with ACSF proximally in s. pyramidale of CA1 just below the surface of the tissue.
source: Field Inhibitory Postsynaptic Potentials (fIPSPs) were evoked by inserting a concentric bipolar stimulating electrode (FHC Inc) and an extracellular recording electrode filled with ACSF (resistance, 1–2 MΩ) proximally in s. pyramidale of CA1 just below the surface of the tissue Younts et al., 2016.
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the experimental procedures.

claim: Paired pulse ratio was measured by eliciting paired-pulse stimulations at decreasing interstimulus intervals (ISIs) of 500, 400, 300, 200, 100, 50, 20 and 30 ms.
source: In all experiments, paired pulse ratio was measured by eliciting paired-pulse stimulations at decreasing interstimulus intervals (ISIs) of 500, 400, 300, 200, 100, 50, 20 and 30 ms.
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the experimental procedures.

claim: The fIPSP peak amplitude of pulse 2 (P2) was divided by pulse 1 (P1) to give a ratio representing presynaptic release probability.
source: The fIPSP peak amplitude of pulse 2 (P2) was divided by pulse 1 (P1) to give a ratio representing presynaptic release probability.
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing how release probability was assessed.

claim: Baseline responses were collected every 10 s (0.1 Hz) using an input stimulus intensity that induced 75% of the slice's maximum response for 10 min.
source: Baseline responses were then collected every 10 s (0.1 Hz) using an input stimulus intensity that induced 75% of the slice's maximum response for 10 min.
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the experimental procedures.

claim: mIPSC decay time is decreased following PTX treatment (paired t-test t(11) = 9.055, p<0.0001, n = 12).
source: mIPSC decay time is decreased following PTX treatment (paired t-test t(11) = 9.055, p<0.0001, n = 12).
evidence: This is a statistical result from experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Evoked response decay time is decreased following PTX treatment (paired t-test t(12) = 6.097, p<0.0001, n = 13).
source: Evoked response decay time is decreased following PTX treatment (paired t-test t(12) = 6.097, p<0.0001, n = 13).
evidence: This is a statistical result from experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: PTX blocks evoked response as a function of stimulation number, rather than time, indicating it is a use-dependent blocker.
source: PTX blocks evoked response as a function of stimulation number, rather than time, indicating it is a use-dependent blocker (non-linear regression single exponential fit for conditions with PTX; Time: Sum-of-Squares F test F(6, 141)=38.16, p<0.0001 that is one curve does not fit all datasets; Stimulation number: Sum-of-Squares F test F(6, 141)=1.005, p=0.4243 that is one curve does fit all datasets, n = 5 all groups).
